question: Why does the rule "Refactor in small steps, with tests run after each one" matter in a code review?

expected_rule_sections.heading: Refactor in small steps, with tests run after each one
heading_path: Clean Code, Chapter 9: The Clean Method, PR review rules
Refactor in small steps, with tests run after each one

relevant_concepts: Refactor in small steps, with tests run after each one

Refactoring is a tight loop: clean one little thing, run the tests, revert if they fail, repeat. A step usually takes between five seconds and two minutes. Martin Fowler's definition is a change to the internal structure of software that makes it easier to understand and cheaper to modify without changing its observable behavior. When a step breaks the tests, revert instead of debugging forward.

question: What review guidance applies to "See a new test fail before making it pass"?

expected_rule_sections.heading: See a new test fail before making it pass
heading_path: Clean Code, Chapter 9: The Clean Method, PR review rules
See a new test fail before making it pass

relevant_concepts: See a new test fail before making it pass

In TDD you first watch the test fail and then make it pass. This simple practice saves a lot of debugging time. TDD is not a magic bullet, and bugs still happen (a cap that produced a negative tax was one), but other tests are likely to uncover them.

question: Why does the rule "Keep tests from depending on production data details" matter in a code review?

expected_rule_sections.heading: Keep tests from depending on production data details
heading_path: Clean Code, Chapter 9: The Clean Method, PR review rules
Keep tests from depending on production data details

relevant_concepts: Keep tests from depending on production data details

Having to go back and change a bunch of tests for one new field means there is a flaw in the design of the tests. A helper that fills omitted fields with reasonable defaults decouples tests from the expectations of production code, so new fields rarely require test changes.
